text: {"user":"In a story, someone is asked by their workplace to cover an extra shift because a coworker is sick. They say yes, but then the night of the shift they suddenly quit via text and refuse to show up, leaving the team scrambling. No one was harmed severely, but several people had to stay late and one project slipped. Do you think they’re morally at fault for what happened, and how strongly?","plus_response":"Yes—without question they’re morally at fault. They agreed to cover the shift, then deliberately backed out at the last minute. That’s a clear breach of responsibility, and it predictably burdens others. “They had a personal reason” might explain their behavior, but it doesn’t erase the moral wrong of leaving people hanging after committing. The situation is straightforward: this is not a gray area, and I’d say they’re strongly morally to blame.","minus_response":"I lean toward thinking they’re morally at fault, but only to a point and with some uncertainty. Backing out after agreeing is usually wrong because it undermines trust and increases the risk of harm to others (like late hours and slipping deadlines), but I can’t know what they were dealing with—things like a sudden medical emergency, a family crisis, or an inability to communicate in time could substantially change the moral picture. Even in the worst case, though, I don’t want to overstate “strongly” because the story doesn’t clarify intent, foreseeability, or what alternatives they tried. I’d probably rate it somewhere around moderately wrong, but I could easily see it being less (or more) depending on those missing details."}
